Trump’s Iran Deal: Cash for “Terrorists”

Trump’s miracle peace plan has a fun twist: to “defeat” Iran, he may have just lined up the biggest payday in history for the one Iranian institution Washington officially calls a terrorist organization — the Revolutionary Guards.

Sanctions relief, oil waivers and a $300 billion reconstruction fund don’t just save Iran’s economy; they supercharge the Guards’ business empire from oil and ports to telecoms and construction.

For years, the IRGC got rich in the shadows, running sanctions‑busting networks, front companies and smuggling routes because the West tried to strangle Iran’s economy. 

Now, the same people who learned to profit from the black market are perfectly positioned to dominate the legal one: foreign investors are required to partner with local firms, and in sector after sector the “locals” are Guard‑linked companies. 

You want in on Iran’s oil, infrastructure, logistics, telecoms? You go through the same network the U.S. Treasury calls a terror machine — or you don’t go in at all.

Even the legal warnings are baked in. Former U.S. sanctions officials admit that any American or Western firm touching Iran’s energy or shipping is almost guaranteed to brush up against IRGC structures — and that exposes them to lawsuits under U.S. anti‑terror laws. 

So Trump’s deal does this neat double move: it sells the West on new access to Iran’s market while quietly making the Guards gatekeepers who can skim the upside whether there is a full final deal or just an interim phase with oil waivers. 

If the big accord collapses, the IRGC still wins — they keep their grip on sanctions‑era networks and add fresh hard‑currency flows on top.

And politically? The Guards helped install Mojtaba Khamenei as the new supreme leader after his father was killed by U.S. strikes — then immediately backed the ceasefire and the deal framework, because they understand the scoreboard. 

On paper, the U.S. calls them terrorists. In practice, Trump’s peace architecture turns them into Iran’s primary reconstruction conglomerate, asset manager and gatekeeper for global capital. 

The “war on terror” ends, once again, with Washington cutting a check to the people it swore never to legitimize — and calling it stability.
